questions.q: What are the five steps of a basic PyTorch training loop, in order?
options: Backward, forward, loss, update, zero gradients
Forward pass, compute loss, zero gradients, backward pass, update parameters
Load data, save model, forward pass, loss, backward pass
Zero gradients, update parameters, forward pass, loss, backward pass
questions.explain: The canonical order is: forward pass (predict), compute loss, zero old gradients, call .backward(), then update parameters. Zeroing must happen before backward, and update happens after.

questions.q: Why is the parameter update step (e.g. `w -= lr * w.grad`) wrapped in torch.no_grad()?
options: To make the update run on the GPU
Because otherwise autograd would try to build a computational graph for the update itself, which is unnecessary and incorrect since we aren't differentiating through the optimization step
Because in-place operations are only allowed inside no_grad()
To silence Python warnings
questions.explain: The update modifies parameter values directly. If this were tracked by autograd, it would build a graph for an operation we never intend to differentiate through, wasting memory and risking errors on in-place modification of a leaf tensor.

questions.q: In the from-scratch training loop, what does setting w.grad = None (or calling zero_grad) immediately before loss.backward() accomplish?
options: It resets the model's weights to their initial random values
It clears gradients left over from the previous iteration so the new backward pass doesn't accumulate on top of stale values
It disables gradient tracking for the rest of the loop
It has no effect since gradients reset automatically
questions.explain: Gradients accumulate in .grad across backward() calls. Setting .grad to None (or zeroing it) clears the previous iteration's values so the new backward pass starts from a clean slate.

questions.q: In the linear regression example, what is the best signal that training is actually working?
options: The script runs without throwing an exception
The loss steadily decreases over epochs, and the learned w and b approach the true values used to generate the data
The learning rate increases automatically
The tensors move from CPU to GPU
questions.explain: The most useful debugging signal in training is whether the loss trends downward. In this synthetic example, we can additionally confirm success because the learned w and b should approach the known true_w and true_b.

questions.q: What role does the learning rate (lr) play in the update step?
options: It determines how many epochs the loop runs for
It scales how large a step each parameter takes against its gradient; too large causes divergence, too small causes very slow progress
It sets the batch size
It controls which device the tensors are created on
questions.explain: The learning rate is the step size multiplying the gradient in the update rule. Too high a value can cause the loss to diverge or oscillate; too low a value makes training very slow to converge.
